summary: Login latency (p99 ~3.8s sustained) and 503s on POST /v1/auth/login began at ~06:54Z and are an overload/queueing signature, not a bad-deployment signature: the auth-service worker pool was pinned at 64/64 with queues up to ~98,763, every 503 is an "accept queue full" rejection, and CPU hit 96-99% with flat memory. The top hypothesis is H3 (genuine login-traffic surge, credential stuffing / retry storm overrunning auth-service capacity with the autoscaler capped at maxReplicas 8) at only 0.45 confidence, driven by the >3x request-rate rise coincident with CPU saturation and the autoscaler's "desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8" message. The reporter's bcrypt-regression hypothesis (H1) is rejected: no auth-service deployment exists in the window and the only auth-service config change is a log.level INFO->WARN edit, while no login-path dependency shows degradation. Because the top hypothesis remains below the confidence threshold and the blast-radius/shared-infrastructure cross-checks were never run, the outcome is recorded as inconclusive with the surge-capacity cause as the leading (unconfirmed) explanation.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Genuine login-traffic surge (credential stuffing / retry storm) overruns auth-service capacity, autoscaler capped
ranked_hypotheses.statement: Login request rate more than tripled, driven by external retry/bot/credential-stuffing traffic (possibly amplified by client retries of the already-slow endpoint). auth-service's provisioned capacity/maxReplicas were insufficient, the autoscaler hit maxReplicas=8-14, workers pinned at 96-99% CPU, the worker queue grew to ~98k, and the accept queue began rejecting with 503s. No faulty code or config change is involved.

causal_chain.claim: External login traffic surge begins ~06:50Z (request_rate 391-411 -> 680 -> ~1450-1520 req/s)
auth-service worker pool saturates (active=64/64, queue depths 3787-98763) and CPU pegs at 96-99%
Timing is consistent with work arriving (queues) — comes as a single step, no dependency slowdown to blame
User-visible symptom: sustained ~3.5-4.0s p99 and 503 accept-queue rejections on /v1/auth/login

assumptions: That the traffic surge is externally generated (the evidence does not distinguish real third-party load from client retry amplification; both are capacity_saturation and would call for the same fix — raise maxReplicas/capacity and/or shed or rate-limit the load).
That request_rate is measured on auth-service itself, not only on the gateway.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared-infrastructure/co-tenant contention (node/sidecar/shared cache) degraded auth-service indirectly
ranked_hypotheses.statement: Something else co-located or shared with auth-service (a node-level stressor, a co-tenant service, a shared proxy/DNS, or the shared redis-cache as a shared resource) degraded at the same time, and auth-service's symptoms are collateral damage rather than an auth-service-local fault. This predicts the same onset pattern in at least one other credential/identity service, and predicts auth-service CPU saturation without a matching auth-service traffic surge (a wildcard not seen): the observed simultaneous 3.5-4x request-rate rise and CPU rise (F10, F11) is more consistent with H3.

causal_chain.claim: A shared node/co-tenant resource degrades (no finding directly shows this)
auth-service CPU/latency rises at the same time

assumptions: That no other service was checked for a matching onset — the blast-radius cross-check was never run, so a shared-infrastructure cause cannot be fully excluded.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Login-path dependency (redis-cache / user-db / kyc-provider) degraded, auth-service is a victim
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A shared downstream dependency on the login path (shared redis-cache, user-db, or the external kyc-provider) became slow, so auth-service login requests queue up and the service saturates while waiting — the 503s/latency are propagated, not locally generated.

causal_chain.claim: auth-service login handlers block on the dependency
request accumulation -> worker pool/accept queue overflow -> 503

assumptions: That a brief saturation of redis-cache or user-db could be missed by the 5-minute/120s bucket averages (partially countered by F13's flat per-minute series).
That kyc-provider degradation could be invisible because it has no telemetry (still open).
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: F13/F17: redis-cache CPU stayed flat 20.6-24% and hit_ratio ~96% through the whole onset; user-db slow_queries_per_min stayed flat at 0.18-0.51 the entire time (F14). Neither dependency shows latency, error or saturation. F16/F15/F10: auth-service latency and CPU jump as a single local step at its own CPU saturation, not a gradual ramp that would follow a downstream slowdown. The only rising upstream-facing metric (user-db connections_active, F14) rises simultaneously with auth CPU, consistent with auth-service driving the extra load itself. F17 states this inference.

ranked_hypotheses.title: auth-service release reintroduced bcrypt cost regression (reporter's hypothesis)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: An auth-service code release raised the bcrypt cost factor (or otherwise made password verification CPU-bound), so login verification burns CPU, saturates the worker pool / accept queue, and produces 3.8s p99 plus 503s — the same mechanism as HIST-101 in 2025-08.

causal_chain.claim: auth-service deploy raises bcrypt cost factor
verifyPassword becomes CPU-bound, auth-service CPU pegged

assumptions: That the bcrypt cost is a deploy-time constant and cannot change without a release (true for HIST-101's mechanism).
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: F1: the deployment inventory shows NO auth-service deployment anywhere in 2026-04-16 -> 2026-04-22 (count 0), and the only deployment fleet-wide is portfolio-service. F2: the only auth-service config change is a log.level INFO->WARN verbosity change, not a crypto/bcrypt parameter. F4 states this explicitly. The bcrypt mechanism requires a release to raise the cost factor; no such release exists in the window, so the reporter's mechanism cannot be the origin.

facts.statement: auth-service p99 latency was flat ~85-95ms until 06:53Z, then jumped at 06:54Z to 3849.2ms and stayed ~3.5-4.0s through 08:59Z (the 4s bucket value at 06:52 is a bucket artifact).

Every 503 on POST /v1/auth/login is logged as an overload rejection: top error pattern 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503', count=372, first_seen 06:55:42Z, last 08:58:57Z; error_rate rose from ~0.2% at 06:48 to ~14% sustained.

At onset the auth-service worker pool was fully saturated with a large waiting backlog: 32 WARN 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=...)' entries from 06:54:53Z with queue depths 3787-98763; the first 503 at 06:55:42Z is the accept-queue-full rejection that follows.

auth-service CPU saturates simultaneously with the latency jump (cpu_pct ~37-40% through 06:45, then avg 71.88/max 96.96 at 06:50 and 96-98% onward, max 99.54) while memory_pct stays flat ~51-53% — a CPU-bound signature with no memory growth.

auth-service request_rate more than tripled at onset (~391-411 req/s baseline to avg 680.57/max 1012.36 at 06:50 and ~1450-1520 req/s sustained), and the autoscaler could not absorb it: 'desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further' (first 06:57:15Z, count=4).
Login-path dependencies show no degradation at onset: redis-cache cpu_pct flat 20.59-23.97% and hit_ratio ~94.4-97.3% across 06:40-07:20; user-db slow_queries_per_min flat at 0.18-0.51 throughout.

user-db connections_active rose from ~25 (06:40-06:50) to avg 73.31 at 06:52 and ~79 sustained — simultaneous with auth-service CPU, consistent with auth-service driving the extra connections rather than a downstream slowdown.
No auth-service deployment exists anywhere in the 2026-04-16T00:00Z -> 2026-04-22T08:59Z window (count 0); the only deployment fleet-wide is portfolio-service.
The only config change touching auth-service in the window is cfg-2801: log.level INFO->WARN at 2026-04-22T03:40:00Z — a logging verbosity change, not an auth/bcrypt/crypto parameter.

The historical bcrypt precedent HIST-101 matches the current symptom signature but required a release (v6.4.0) to raise the bcrypt cost factor; no such release exists in this window, so the deployment-driven mechanism cannot be the origin of this incident.

auth-service's login path depends on user-db, redis-cache (marked shared, used by several services), the external kyc-provider (has_telemetry=false), and is called by api-gateway; redis-cache's shared nature is a candidate vector for externally originating damage.

assumptions: That the observed request-rate surge is externally generated traffic; the evidence does not distinguish genuine third-party load from client retry amplification of the already-slow endpoint (both are capacity_saturation and call for the same fix).
That request_rate is measured on auth-service itself and not only at the gateway (the metric was read from auth-service telemetry).
That auth-service capacity in this incident is governed by maxReplicas=8 as reported by the autoscaler, and that replicas could not be increased beyond it in the observed window.

That no relevant change occurred on a login-path dependency that the fleet-wide deployment/config query failed to surface for a specific dependency, and that kyc-provider (no telemetry) did not degrade.
That the 5-minute/120s metric buckets would have surfaced a dependency-side saturation if one existed, i.e. that redis-cache/user-db flatness is not masking a short saturation.
That the traffic surge and CPU saturation are causally related (surge drives CPU), rather than an unrelated CPU burner coinciding with a traffic rise.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) The bcrypt-regression signature is not distinguishable from observed data: CPU is pegged at 96-99% with flat memory (consistent with CPU-bound work in general) but no metric separates verifyPassword CPU from other CPU, and the visible evidence is an overload/queueing signature rather than a per-hash CPU-time signature.

timeline.event: cfg-2801: auth-service log.level changed INFO->WARN by config-bot ('Reduce log volume') — the only auth-service config change in the window, and a non-crypto parameter.
Baseline: auth-service request_rate ~391-411 req/s, CPU ~37-40%, p99 latency ~85-95ms.
CPU begins to rise (120s bucket avg 71.88, max 96.96) as request_rate climbs (avg 680.57, max 1012.36) — onset of the traffic surge and CPU saturation.
auth-service CPU saturates in the 120s bucket (avg 96.89, max 96.96); user-db connections_active jumps ~25 -> avg 73.31 — one bucket before the measured latency jump.
p99 latency jumps in a single step to 3849.2ms and stays ~3.5-4.0s; worker pool saturates (active=64/64) with queue depths 3787-98763 (first WARN 06:54:53Z).
First 503 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)'; error_rate rises from ~0.2% to ~14% sustained.
Autoscaler logs 'desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further' (count=4) — capacity ceiling prevents absorption of the surge.
Throughout the incident window, redis-cache CPU stays ~22% with ~96% hit ratio and user-db slow_queries_per_min stays ~0.2-0.5 — no dependency-side saturation or latency signature.
Last of 372 accept-queue-full 503 rejections logged on POST /v1/auth/login; latency/errors still elevated at latest data (08:59Z).

recommended_actions.action: Raise auth-service capacity / the autoscaler ceiling: increase the maxReplicas setting above 8 (autoscaler was requesting 14) for the auth-service deployment and verify HPA/target metrics so replicas can actually be added; confirm the cap change takes effect during the ongoing elevated request_rate.
recommended_actions.rationale: The autoscaler explicitly could not scale (desired 14 > maxReplicas 8) while request_rate was ~1450-1520 req/s and workers were pinned at 96-99% CPU with queue depths up to 98763 — the direct capacity bottleneck.

recommended_actions.action: Apply rate limiting / load shedding at api-gateway or the auth-service front door for POST /v1/auth/login (and enable/verify the auth-service rate_limited_per_min control), prioritizing real user logins and dropping bot/retry traffic, to relieve accept-queue pressure.
recommended_actions.rationale: All 372 503s are accept-queue-full overload rejections on the login endpoint; shedding excess load is a safe mitigation that does not depend on knowing whether the surge is external or retry-amplified.

recommended_actions.action: Run the blast-radius cross-check: compare request_rate/CPU/latency onset in the 06:45-07:00Z window for api-gateway and for other services co-located with or sharing redis-cache (call get_service_dependencies on redis-cache, direction=upstream) to determine whether the onset is auth-service-local or shared-infrastructure-driven.
recommended_actions.rationale: H3 (0.45) and H4 (0.20) are not yet discriminated: H4 predicts a matching onset in at least one other credential/identity or co-tenant service, and this cross-check was never run.

recommended_actions.action: Determine whether the request-rate surge is external (bot/credential-stuffing) or client retry amplification of the slow endpoint — inspect caller/IP/source distribution, user-agent patterns, and login-failure vs login-success ratios in the auth-service and api-gateway access data for 06:50-08:59Z.
recommended_actions.rationale: The evidence does not distinguish third-party load from client retry amplification; the distinction is needed to choose between bot mitigation and client-side backoff changes, and to confirm H3's causal story.

recommended_actions.action: After capacity mitigation, verify recovery: confirm p99 latency returns to baseline (~85-95ms), error_rate returns to ~0.2%, accept-queue-full 503 count stops incrementing, and worker queue depths return to normal; keep the maxReplicas/capacity change in place and tune autoscaling thresholds from the observed surge profile.
recommended_actions.rationale: Validates that capacity, not a code/config defect, was the binding constraint and closes the loop on the observed queueing and CPU saturation.

recommended_actions.action: Establish guardrails to prevent recurrence: load-test auth-service to the new capacity envelope, set alerting on worker-pool queue depth / accept-queue rejections and on autoscaler maxReplicas saturation, add login-endpoint rate limiting and bot/credential-stuffing protection, and add a CPU-time-by-code-path metric to separate verifyPassword cost from other handler work.
recommended_actions.rationale: The incident showed no early-warning alert before queue depths reached tens of thousands, autoscaling silently capped, and no metric can separate bcrypt/verify-password CPU from other CPU — a gap that made the reporter's bcrypt hypothesis (H1) unfalsifiable from the available data.

recommended_actions.action: Additionally instrument and collect telemetry (or a substitute health signal) for kyc-provider (external, has_telemetry=false) and per-endpoint/health-check latency for auth-service, and backfill the missing deployment/config history before 2026-04-16T00:00Z for user-db and redis-cache.
recommended_actions.rationale: These were explicit gaps: no telemetry for kyc-provider, no per-endpoint latency metrics, and no change history older than ~3.5 days — each leaves a login-path cause channel unchecked.

data_gaps: Could not run the upstream dependency query for redis-cache (get_service_dependencies, direction=upstream) — rejected with budget_exhausted — so the caller list for the shared redis-cache and whether other callers changed is unknown; the shared-infrastructure hypothesis H4 remains unverified.

Deployment/config history for user-db, redis-cache, api-gateway and kyc-provider was not enumerated as separate per-service queries; only fleet-wide scope queries ran (returning just portfolio-service deployment and cfg-2801). A dependency-specific change could be missed.

No deployment/config history exists for the 24-72h before 2026-04-16T00:00Z, so a slower-burning change older than ~3.5 days (e.g. user-db schema/index migration, redis caching-layer config) affecting login is unchecked.
kyc-provider is external with has_telemetry=false, so no deployment, config or metric data can confirm whether it changed or degraded.

Per-endpoint and health-check latency metrics were not available; only overall latency_p99_ms and error_rate exist, so the 'login-only vs all-endpoints' and 'health checks unaffected' conclusions rest on log evidence alone.
No cross-service comparison was run for other services in the 06:45-07:00Z window, so whether any other service shows a matching onset (blast radius) is unanswered.
auth-service logs (06:45-07:10Z: 84 matched/40 shown) and the ERROR query (372 matched/30 shown) were truncated, so a rarer error signature or a deploy/restart marker could be missed.
No CPU-time-by-code-path metric exists for auth-service (verifyPassword vs other handlers), so the bcrypt/verify-password CPU contribution cannot be positively confirmed or ruled out.
redis-cache connected_clients/evictions_per_min and user-db cpu_pct/replication_lag_ms were not queried, so less-common dependency saturation modes were not verified.
Tool reliability: query_metrics(redis-cache, available_metrics) and query_metrics(user-db, available_metrics) both FAILED with not_found, limiting visibility into those dependencies' metric catalogs.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: A successful cross-service comparison showing a matching latency/CPU onset in api-gateway or another co-tenant/credential service in the same 06:45-07:00Z window would support or overturn H4 over H3 (shifting weight toward shared-infrastructure contention).

Evidence that the request-rate surge is entirely client-side retry amplification rather than external bot/credential-stuffing traffic would reframe the cause but still point to the same capacity_saturation fix.
Discovery of an auth-service release or a bcrypt/crypto config change outside the queried window (e.g. older than 2026-04-16) would revive the reporter's H1 bcrypt-regression hypothesis.

Detection of elevated latency, errors or saturation on redis-cache, user-db or kyc-provider at onset (e.g. connection exhaustion, evictions, replication lag, or a kyc-provider slowdown) would support H2 (dependency failure) and point away from the local capacity cause.
A per-endpoint metric showing elevated latency on non-login endpoints or on health checks would argue against a login-path-specific surge and toward a broader/service-wide or node-level cause.
Evidence that replicas were in fact not capped (e.g. the maxReplicas=8 message was stale or not binding) would weaken the capacity-saturation mechanism underlying H3.

findings.statement: No auth-service deployment exists anywhere in the 2026-04-16T00:00Z -> 2026-04-22T08:59Z window (and none in the narrower 2026-04-19T07:00Z -> 2026-04-22T08:59Z window either): get_deployments for auth-service returned count 0, and the all-services query returned a single deployment belonging to portfolio-service.

The only config change in the whole window that touches auth-service is cfg-2801: key log.level changed INFO->WARN at 2026-04-22T03:40:00Z by config-bot ('Reduce log volume') — a logging verbosity change, not an auth/bcrypt/crypto parameter. No other config changes exist fleet-wide in the window.

The historical bcrypt precedent HIST-101 (2025-08-14) has the same symptom signature as the current report — 'login p99 4s', '503 on login', 'high cpu' — with root cause 'bcrypt cost factor raised 10->14 in release v6.4.0', category bad_deployment, resolved by 'Rolled back v6.4.0'. It is a matching lead only, not current evidence.

auth-service latency is flat ~85-94ms for 06:40-06:52 and then jumps in one step to ~3.5-4.0s sustained through 07:20 (min 83.49, max 4015.31) - a local step change at its own CPU saturation, not a gradual ramp consistent with a downstream dependency slowing down.

This points to a locally-caused (in-auth-service) saturation rather than downstream-propagated latency.

The bcrypt-regression signature (slowness concentrated in password-verification CPU time) is NOT distinguishable from the observed data because auth-service CPU is pegged at 96-99% while memory stays flat - consistent with CPU-bound work in general - but no metric separates verifyPassword CPU from other CPU; the queue-saturation logs (active=64/64, queues up to 98763) and the 372 accept-queue-full 503s reported by T1 are an overload/queueing signature rather than a per-hash CPU-time signature. Ruling out blocked/waiting: no dependency shows elevated latency or saturation to blame, and auth CPU saturates simultaneously.
